Senior leaders had overlooked or were unaware of multiple areas of fundamental standards. This included policies and procedures, fire safety, staff supervision, and the management of incidents, especially medicines incidents. Senior leaders had not been aware that there were shortfalls in the service regarding safe recruitment processes for staff, risk management for clients, and discharge planning. However, clients and staff did state that the senior leaders worked hard and were approachable.

We informed the provider of our serious concerns during and immediately after this inspection. We sent a letter of intent (notice of CQC’s intention to take urgent action) to the provider about our concerns in relation to the leadership of the service. The provider sent us an action plan to address our concerns, and to provide assurances of how the risks identified have already been removed or are immediately being removed within a certain timeframe. Since our inspection, the provider has advertised for a new Registered Manager. We will re-inspect this service in the near future to ensure the changes have been implemented.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Freedom to speak up

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service did not create a positive culture where people feel that they can speak up and that their voice will be heard.

Staff said they felt confident in raising concerns about poor professional practice or inappropriate conduct, however, there were insufficient policies or practice in place to support this appropriately. The service did not have a whistleblowing policy in place, or equivalent. The service did not have a Freedom to Speak Up Guardian. The pathway for managing staff concerns was not documented well, clearly investigated, or evidenced that feedback was provided to staff about the outcome or lessons learned.

Additionally, we saw evidence that staff had reported to senior leaders around concerns around admissions happening all at one time, as they could be distracting to staff at key points of the day such as medicine’s administration time but saw no evidence that senior leaders were putting processes in place to ensure this occurred.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Governance, management and sustainability

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service did not have clear responsibilities, roles, systems of accountability and good governance to manage and deliver good quality, sustainable care, treatment and support.

Senior leaders did not have a clear understanding, oversight or embedded governance systems for the service. This included the model of care, client risks, policies and procedures, managing mixed-sex accommodation, safeguarding, incidents, complaints, risk management, maintaining a safe and secure environment, fire safety, safe staff recruitment, staff training, supervision, and medicines management.

The service did not carry out any governance meetings. There was only a monthly team meeting, which followed a basic agenda and did not share any data on the service or lessons learned from incidents or complaints raised by clients or staff from the previous month. We found no evidence that lessons learned were shared with staff efficiently or that senior leaders had implemented recommendations. For example, all staff support medicines administration, but some staff we spoke to were unaware of the multiple medicines incidents that have occurred in the service, which also involved controlled drugs.

The service did not have a risk register. We identified multiple areas of risk for the service, including, but not limited to, compliance with fire regulations, risk management of clients, mixed-sex accommodation, staff supervision and training, and policies and procedures.

The service did not have plans for emergencies. The service did not have a business continuity plan in place to cover eventualities such as adverse weather or a flu outbreak. The service did not have personal emergency evacuation plans (PEEPS) for clients in the event of a fire.

Staff did not undertake appropriate audits to ensure safe and quality care was being provided. Audits that did take place, were not carried out at the required frequency or correctly. For example, only one monthly medicines audit had taken place in the 8 months since the service had been registered, but there were multiple medicines incidents. The weekly health and safety audit had identified that fire safety equipment and processes were in place, but the service had not conducted one fire safety check since the service registered. Thus, the audits were not sufficient to provide assurance to senior leaders, and there was no evidence that senior leaders had acted on any results when needed.

Senior leaders did not have access to information to support them with their management role. This included information on the performance of the service, staffing and client care.

Staff could not explain how they were working to deliver care and treatment within the client’s cost of care and treatment. For example, the service advertises free aftercare group sessions, as part of any admission cost. However, staff told us that some counsellors work privately outside of the service, and that sometimes clients continue working with those counsellors after they have left the service. Senior leaders told us this is booked and paid directly to TLC rehab, who then pays the counselling staff. It is unclear how this is arranged, if this is part of the aftercare package, and if not, why payment goes through TLC Rehab, instead of directly to the counsellors.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Learning, improvement and innovation

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service did not focus on continuous learning, innovation and improvement.

There was one quality improvement (QI) project in the service. This was around implementing the not 12-step model approach to addiction. However, the service had been open for 8 months, and the model of care was still not clear or embedded.

The service did not share lessons learnt with staff or implement actions following incidents.

Staff have not participated in national audits relevant to the service.

The service has not participated in accreditation schemes relevant to the service.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Partnerships and communities

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service did not understand their duty to collaborate and work in partnership. The service did not share information and learning with partners and collaborate for improvement.

The service did not work well with other agencies such as health and social care professionals and the local authority safeguarding team. Since the service registered it has not made any safeguarding referrals to the local authority, despite there being a need to. We also saw clients who would benefit from alternative placements due to the primary concern for treatment not being related to substance misuse, but poor mental health. The provider should consider how they will collaborate with key agencies to discuss their inspection action plan, progress that has been made, and any remaining actions.

Clients and staff told us that they could meet with members of the provider’s senior leadership team to give feedback. However, we saw poor evidence of monitoring and investigating feedback and updating clients and staff with the outcomes or lessons learned.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Shared direction and culture

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service did not have a shared vision, strategy and culture that is based on transparency, equity, equality and human rights, diversity and inclusion, engagement, and understanding and meeting the needs of people and our communities.

This is the first inspection of the service since it registered in September 2024. The service did not have a clear vision, direction or culture. The service stated it was a specialised substance misuse rehabilitation service, specialising in detox, but had admitted clients who did not require a detox.

The provider’s senior leadership team had not successfully communicated the provider’s vision and values to the frontline staff in this service. Team meetings did not have an agenda item, or document any discussion about visions, values or strategy. Staff did not have the opportunity to contribute to discussions about the strategy for the service, especially where the service was changing. Staff told us that during the inspection a senior leader told them that they were planning to expand the service. Staff told us they had not heard this before and were not clear how the service could be expanded.

Although senior staff described providing a non 12 step programme for substance misuse, staff could not clearly describe what this meant and how the care delivered was in line with this approach.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Workforce equality, diversity and inclusion

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service did not always value diversity in their workforce. The service did not work towards an inclusive and fair culture by improving equality and equity for people who worked for them.

There were no key policies and procedures in place in relation to Equality, Diversity and Inclusion. There were no equality and diversity champions within the service e.g. LGBT+, BME etc.

There was no evidence about whether staff were able to apply to work flexibly e.g. flexible working agreements to account for personal circumstances such as caring responsibilities and health issues. We did not see evidence of managers putting reasonable adjustments in place for staff members to help them carry out their role.

The service employed a diverse team of staff from international backgrounds. Staff did not raise any concerns about discrimination.

overall.narrative: The service is performing badly and we've taken action against the person or organisation that runs it.
overall.commentary:
Date of assessment: 9 and 10 July 2025

TLC Rehab is a residential substance misuse rehabilitation service. At the time of our inspection it offered alcohol detoxification, opiate detox, benzodiazepines detox and residential substance misuse rehabilitation. The service had capacity for 10 clients. The accommodation was mixed-sex. There were 8 clients residing at the service at the time of this inspection.

The service registered with the CQC in September 2024. It is registered to deliver the regulated activities of Accommodation for persons who require treatment for substance misuse and Treatment of disease, disorder, or injury. There is a registered manager in place.

We conducted this unannounced assessment in July 2025 to follow up concerns identified in the comprehensive assessment completed in April 2025. TLC Rehab was the only registered location for the provider and was for self-funding clients.

At the previous assessment in April 2025, we found concerns relating to all key questions. As a result, we issued a Section 31 Letter of Intent to the service, outlining our serious concerns and intention to take enforcement action. The service responded by bringing together an action plan to address all areas, with all points to be completed by 30 June 2025. The concerns related to the model of care, inclusion and exclusion criteria, safeguarding, risk management of clients, safe staffing, security of premises, fire safety, governance, outcome measures, policies and procedures, discharge planning and incidents and complaints. We also issued a warning notice around the safe management of medicines.

During this current assessment, we returned to the service to assess the progress against the action plan and to ensure areas of concern had been addressed appropriately. We found that a significant number of actions had not been completed. We found continued areas of concern across all areas of the service that the service had not addressed. We found the warning notice around medicines management was not complied with.

As a result, we took enforcement action and issued a Notice of Decision to impose conditions on the provider’s registration in respect of their regulated activities. We took this urgent action as we believed persons would or may be exposed to the risk of harm if we did not do so.

We imposed the following conditions:

  1. The Registered Provider must not admit any new service user to TLC Rehab from 5pm on the 11 July 2025, until they can demonstrate completion of all necessary actions in relation to areas or concern outlined in the Letter of Intent, dated 2 May 2025.
  2. The Registered Provider must ensure that all current service user’s health and care needs are reviewed immediately, and a copy of this review is sent to the Care Quality Commission by midday on 14 July 2025. Any service user whose needs align with the providers’ exclusion criteria must be informed in writing so they can identify an alternative service where their needs can be safely met. Copies of the correspondence to these service users must be provided to the Commission.

The overall rating for this service remained Inadequate. During this inspection we found continued breaches of regulation. We also found that the requirements of a warning notice around medicines management had not been met.

keyQuestions.commentary:
We looked for evidence that service leadership, management and governance assured high-quality, person-centred care; supported learning and innovation and promoted an open, fair culture.

asgRatings.title: Ongoing Assessment for TLC Rehab - Archived
asgRatings.name: Residential substance misuse services
asgRatings.commentary:
This was the second assessment for this newly registered service. We first inspected the service in April 2025. We found multiple concerns during the April 2025 assessment across all five domains which still remained during this July 2025 assessment. We informed the provider of our serious concerns during and immediately after this assessment.

In April 2025, we sent a letter of intent (notice of CQC’s intention to take urgent action) to the provider about our concerns in relation to; the model of care, inclusion and exclusion criteria, outcomes measures, discharge planning, safeguarding, risk management of clients, policies and procedures, incidents and complaints, safe staffing, security of premises, fire safety, governance and the directors. The provider sent us an action plan to address our concerns outlining how the concerns would be addressed within set timeframes.

This current inspection took place to assess progress against the action plan. We found a significant lack of progress against the plan. As a result, we imposed conditions on the registration of the service (please see the assessment summary section above).

In April 2025 we also served a warning notice around the safe management of medicines. During this current inspection we saw the concerns had not been addressed and the service was not compliant with the notice.

Mental Health Act and Mental Capacity Act Compliance

Mental Health Act

The service did not admit clients under the Mental Health Act 1983. All clients were self-funded.

Although the service did not admit clients under the Mental Health Act 1983, many people in residential substance misuse services have co-occurring mental health conditions (dual diagnosis) or mental health needs, where referral for assessment under the Mental Health Act may be required. Staff had not received training on how to support a client whose mental health was deteriorating in order to refer the person to crisis mental health services if needed. They did not know how the Mental Health Act might be used in these circumstances.

Mental Capacity Act

Most staff had a limited knowledge and understanding of the Mental Capacity Act 2005. In April 2025 we found that 2 of 13 staff had received training in the Mental Capacity Act 2005. There was no evidence that this had changed, at this inspection. The Registered Manager and Nominated Individual had not completed or been booked to receive this training. Clients who access residential substance misuse services can have fluctuating or impaired capacity when under the influence of substances. Staff working in substance misuse services should have received training in the Mental Capacity Act 2005 to ensure they have appropriate knowledge to undertake mental capacity assessments for clients who may have impaired capacity and will need to consent to a variety of decisions, including consent to detoxification, substitute prescribing, unplanned exits from treatment and sharing of information.

The provider had a policy on the Mental Capacity Act. At the last inspection we found no evidence that staff were aware of the policy and had access to it. During this inspection we saw that 9 staff had confirmed electronically that they had seen and read the policy.

The service did not have arrangements in place to monitor adherence to the Mental Capacity Act. There were no audits in regard to application of the Mental Capacity Act and no evidence of lessons learned.

topicareas.name: Assessing needs

evidenceCategory.commentary:
In April 2025 we identified several issues relating to the assessment of need. These issues were in the timeliness of assessments on admission, including risk, physical health and mental health assessments. We saw examples of missing information from assessments which could have resulted in avoidable harm. Not all staff had received training in working in substance misuse services. There was a lack of embedded audit that could be used to identify areas of improvement. The service planned to address this by making the admission policy and decision making around admission more robust, auditing admissions to ensure necessary paperwork was present, and assessing competencies and training needs. During this assessment, we found these actions had not taken place. The admission policy remained unclear about the process to follow when a patient met the exclusion criteria and stated the registered manager could make a final decision about admission, although they did not have the appropriate clinic training and competencies to do this. We saw records of 5 clients who had been admitted without their GP summary being available, and some went on to have hospital admissions due to physical health deterioration. The service had not created or implemented any audits around admission paperwork and practice. Staff had not received training in supporting people receiving care for substance misuse. Only 2 of 4 staff involved in admissions had their competencies around admissions assessed.

There was limited or no record of multidisciplinary team discussion around admissions, including those with complex needs.

Staff assessed clients’ needs for food and drink and for specialist nutrition and hydration. We saw evidence that staff used the Malnutrition Universal Screening Tool (MUST), to assess if clients were malnourished or at risk of malnutrition.

Staff used the NEWS2 scoring system to monitor clients’ physical health regularly.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Consent to care and treatment

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service did not always tell people about their rights around consent and respect these when they delivered person-centred care and treatment.

Staff recorded capacity to consent to treatment and sharing of information for all clients residing at the service. This was completed comprehensively and all had client’s electronic signatures. There were no capacity assessments on file, as all clients were presumed to capacity.

In our April 2025 assessment, we found the service had multiple blanket restrictions in place which were not clearly documented in the client’s treatment agreement. During this inspection, there was no evidence that the service had put in place actions it had outlined to address this. There was no signage to detail the restrictions in place or explanations to why, and we could not see evidence that restrictions or prohibited items were discussed with clients during their admission.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Delivering evidence-based care and treatment

evidenceCategory.commentary:
Staff provided some care and treatment interventions suitable for most of the clients. The care and treatment interventions that TLC Rehab offered were medically monitored pharmacological detox regimes for alcohol, opiate and benzodiazepines addictions, group based psychosocial interventions based around the 12-step principles and one-to-one counselling. These interventions were those recommended by guidance from the Drug misuse and dependence: UK guidelines on clinical management and National Institute for Health and Care Excellence. The documentation around the model of care had been updated to indicate that a doctor was not on site at all times.

The service provided individual and group therapeutic intervention as well as therapeutic activities such as a walk and talk group, nutrition group and a client led yoga group. The lead therapist who had devised the therapeutic programme and led on delivering it was leaving the service in the two weeks after the inspection and the service did not have a clear plan in place to minimise disruption to clients and ensure continuation of care.

In the 9 care records we looked at, 3 clients did not have evidence of care plans. Good practice indicates that care plans are important to outline how staff can support clients to have safe and effective care. Care plans can identify agreed upon goals, include a person's strengths and should be developed jointly with them. Without a care plan, the service cannot demonstrate how they are identifying and meeting the needs of individual clients. For 2 clients, these care plans were created 6 days after their admission, which meant staff would not have a clear and consistent plan of support before this time.

Clients were not offered routine screening for blood borne viruses, which NICE guidelines state that services should focus on. The service did not offer routine pregnancy tests for clients who may need one.

At the inspection in April 2025, we identified a blanket restriction for all clients on kitchen access. All clients were low risk, and the service hoped to focus on rehabilitation and support with life skills, and a restriction on kitchen access did not seem to support this model of care. During this inspection, we saw there had been no change to this, and no evidence of consideration of this by the service.

Clients’ physical healthcare was managed by their GP. Staff assessed client’s core physical health needs on admission, and this was reviewed throughout their stay. This included an assessment of temperature, pulse, blood pressure, weight, a breathalyser and urine test. If any further physical assessment or tests were required, clients needed to access a walk-in centre, or A&E department, or register temporarily with a local GP.

At the April 2025 inspection, we identified that staff participated in some audits, but these were not completed correctly, routinely or in a timely manner. During this inspection, there was no evidence that this had been addressed. There were no audits available.

Although the team included or had access to most specialists required to meet the needs of clients in the service, clients did not have access to occupational therapists, social workers, or peer support workers, which would support holistic rehabilitation.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: How staff, teams and services work together

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service held monthly team meetings and fortnightly therapy team meetings. Staff also had a daily handover meeting when shifts changed. At the assessment in April 2025, we found that meeting minutes did not contain sufficient information for staff to read, understand, make any improvements, or to check back that actions had been made. Handover minutes did not make clear how identified risks and actions were updated on patient care records or assigned to staff to ensure they took place.

During this assessment, we found no consistent improvement to minutes, including handovers. The action plan outlined that the registered manager would hold two team meetings per week, to discuss any changes to existing policies and practice. We saw evidence of only three meetings taking place between 29 April and 8 July 2025.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Monitoring and improving outcomes

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service had an outcomes policy in place, although this did not have a date of creation or commencement. There was no evidence available that this had been shared with staff to ensure they were aware of the policy.

Although staff used a range of recognised rating scales to assess and record the severity of clients’ conditions at admission and at different times during their treatment, this was not done consistently. We saw that staff used tools including the Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol (CIWA) to assess and monitor the severity of alcohol withdrawal symptoms, the Severity of Alcohol Dependence Questionnaire (SADQ), to assess the severity of psychological and physical dependence on alcohol and the Recovery Assessment Scale with 41 items (RAS-41), to measure progress in recovery. We also saw that staff used the Malnutrition Universal Screening Tool (MUST) to assess if clients were malnourished or at risk of malnutrition.

The service did not use data from outcome measures well, in order to monitor successful treatment and drive service development and improvement.

Following the April 2025 assessment, the service action plan outlined that the leadership staff would create and implement a weekly outcomes audit, as well as include this as a topic in a monthly governance audit. During this inspection, there was no evidence that this audit documentation had been created, and no evidence that any audits had been carried out.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Supporting people to live healthier lives

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service aimed to provide facilities and activities to support people to live healthier lives. There was a large garden for clients to use, and this had a table tennis table available. One of the therapists also led a weekly yoga session. There was a walk and talk group for clients to participate in, and staff said they would risk assess if someone was able to go out jogging. Therapy staff said they asked about activities that people enjoyed and tried to support them to continue to access these.

The service contracted services of a nutritionist, who could come to the service once a week.

The service did not provide information about the other ways it could have supported clients to live healthier loves. For example, through participation in smoking cessation schemes, managing cardiovascular risks, or national screenings for cancer.

topicareas.name: Care provision, Integration and continuity

evidenceCategory.commentary:
Staff supported clients to maintain contact with their families and carers. Clients were able to communicate via their mobile phones and laptops.

The service did not provide clients with information about or access to education and work opportunities as part of their care and treatment at the service, or as part of their discharge plan.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Equity in access

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service had a website with clear information about what it offered and how to make a self-referral, but it did not have clear procedures for staff to follow when the service could not meet someone's needs. For example, what information to share about why their needs could not be met and alternative pathways or services. Senior leaders confirmed they did not record data about referrals it could not accept, and were not able to describe what information would be given to these people to advise on alternative pathways or services. For clients that had been accepted, they were able to access the service in a timescale that suited them.

The service was not proactive in collecting information about the community it serviced, in order to improve access for marginalised groups.

The service environment met the accessibility needs of its current clients. The service was based across three floors. The service had a lift to ensure clients with mobility issues could have equity in access. The service had multiple ground floor bedrooms if required.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Equity in experiences and outcomes

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service did not actively seek out and listen to information about people who are most likely to experience inequality in experience or outcomes.

Concerns identified in April 2025 remained.

Staff within the service did not always promote a culture in which the people using the service felt empowered to give their views. The service held inconsistent community meetings, which clients stated they wanted, in order to discuss key topics such as the environment and food choices. The service had decided not to implement these more frequently since April 2025, despite receiving this feedback.

The provider had not undertaken equality impact assessments of their policies and procedures to ensure they did not place vulnerable people or people with protected characteristics at a disadvantage.

Staff were not trained in equality, diversity, inclusion and human rights (EDIHR) and the service had no policy in relation to EDIHR.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Listening to and involving people

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service did not always make it easy for people to share feedback and ideas or raise complaints about their care, treatment and support and receive an appropriate response.

Clients knew how to complain or raise concerns and had access to the complaints procedure. We saw the complaints procedure on the noticeboard and in the admissions pack.

In April 2025, we found poor monitoring and investigation of complaints. During this inspection we found this had not improved. Senior leaders told us that there had been no complaints since April 2025 and there were none on the complaints log. However, in other documentation relating to patient care, we saw references to patient complaints. Some of these complaints referred to staff conduct and patients feeling unsafe. One member of staff told us patients had complained to them about aspects of their care recently, and this had not been recorded as a formal complaint by senior staff.

We found no evidence that clients or staff received feedback on the outcome of investigations of complaints and acted on the findings.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Person-centred Care

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The therapy and nursing team met with clients to understand their views on care and treatment. These discussions took place in their one-to-one meetings. Staff monitored clients’ conditions and discussed any changes at handover meetings.

In the care records we looked at, we saw a variation in how personalised records were. We saw some examples where records were personalised and reflected the client’s personal preferences or wishes. For example, personalised treatment goals written clearly. We saw others where more personalised information would have supported better care. For example, more information about personal triggers and how staff could respond to these.

Two chefs worked at the service and delivered a different meal plan each week. They could amend the menu if requested. They were able to cater for different dietary needs and had clear information about allergies.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Planning for the future

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service did not actively support people to understand and make decisions about their future care and support, including those relating to potential medical and psychological needs.

Concerns relating to this area identified in April 2025 remained. The service could not provide evidence that the actions required in their action plan had been done.

Most clients records we reviewed did not have clear discharge plans in place. There was no clear evidence that the team working collaboratively with clients and their carers when planning for each client’s discharge and return to their local area.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Providing Information

evidenceCategory.commentary:
Staff provided clients general information on the service and activities through a welcome pack and notice boards throughout the service. This information was presented in standard English, but staff could source this in other languages or formats if needed. Since the April 2025 assessment, the service had updated the client information pack to include information about keys to bedrooms and safe spaces for possessions.

Staff had access to the equipment and information technology needed to do their work.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

keyQuestionRatings.name: Safe
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
We looked for evidence on how the service provided safe care and treatment, and evidence that people were protected from abuse and avoidable harm.

This key question has been rated inadequate. This meant people were not safe and were at risk of avoidable harm. The concerns that we found in April 2025 had not been sufficiently addressed and remained in place. We found breaches of regulation in relation to this key question.

Clients had been admitted without full information from the GP and medical history, which is not best practice, and several clients had been admitted to hospital with deteriorating health needs. Incidents were not reported or investigated thoroughly, and the service did not take proportionate actions in response to the incidents or share lessons learned. Our concerns around medicines management had not been addressed and we saw some of these concerns repeated, which indicated no learning had taken place. The service had a lack of oversight of several staffing areas, including staff training and supervision.

topicareas.name: Infection prevention and control

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service did not always assess and manage the risk of infection and detect and control the risk of it spreading, as well as it could have done.

The service was mostly clean, well-decorated, had good furnishings and was broadly fit for purpose. External cleaners attended the service three times a week and kept cleaning records which were up-to-date. However, we observed the ground floor bath and areas of the kitchen to be visibly dirty. Senior leaders were aware of concerns around the cleanliness of the kitchen and had spoken to the chef around this. Senior leaders told us that a deep clean for the service had been booked.

Most staff had completed infection prevention and control training Levels 1 and 2, however there were no completion or renewal dates available. Only 1 senior leader was listed to have completed the training.

Food was cooked by an employed chef. However, we observed that staff were involved with the handling of food and not all staff had completed food hygiene and food safety training. A newly recruited service manager had recognised a need for cleaning wipes and gloves for staff when preparing food and had recently implemented this.

We saw that food was mostly stored in line with food safety standards. The service had allergy stickers, food date stickers, and guidance on safe storage was present on the kitchen walls. However weekly infection control audits had identified that food labels were not always used on all opened food items. Audits also identified that the Food Standards Agency Manual was not always completed daily. Despite audits identifying these concerns, no actions were listed or evidenced that it had been shared with the staff team.

Clients were not able to access the kitchen, but there was a fridge and microwave in the communal dining area that they could use to store and heat food.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Involving people to manage risks

evidenceCategory.commentary:
We reviewed the care records for 9 clients who were currently using the service or recently discharged.

Staff completed a variety of risk assessments for clients on admission, but these were not always kept up-to-date or hold all relevant information. The assessments carried out included an overall risk assessment, drug/alcohol assessment, physical health assessment and mental health assessment. In 2 records, we saw that staff did not update these after an incident took place. This meant they may not have the most up-to-date information about risk or how to manage and mitigate this. For 2 clients, we saw risks identified that did not have suitable plans in place for management. For example, one person who needed support with housing, and one person who needed an additional falls assessment to help manage their mobility appropriately. For 1 patient, a physical health condition that was referenced in other parts of their notes was not clear in their risk assessment and did not have a management plan in place, which it should have done. For another patient, their severe allergy was not made clear in all the appropriate areas of their care notes.

At the inspection in April 2025, we found no records of aftercare or discharge for patients. During this inspection, we saw 1 client had clear information about their discharge plans recorded. For others, we did not see clear information recorded. This included information about triggers for individuals that may lead to unplanned discharges, or how staff could manage this. After this inspection, the service stated information around planning for discharge was in the patient care records, but acknowledged the structure and clarity of discharge information could be improved.

The service employed an advocacy service that clients could access. Information about this and how to access it was only available in the admission packs.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Learning culture

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service did not have a proactive and positive culture of safety based on openness and honesty, in which concerns about safety were listened to, safety events were investigated, reported thoroughly, and lessons learned to continually identify and embed good practices.

During our assessment in April 2025, we found concerns under this quality statement. During this inspection, we found that most concerns had not been addressed, although a small number of areas were improved.

During this inspection we found that staff could explain what incidents to report. Staff were required to notify senior leaders of incidents, who were then responsible for recording them in an incident log and carrying out any necessary investigations. We found a delay in the recording of and investigation of multiple incidents, a lack of urgency to implement mitigations to risks, and a lack of support for the clients around the incidents. For example, there had been an incident in the previous weeks involving a young person from next door accessing the garden and attempting to sell drugs to the clients. Clients stated that this impacted their well-being. Senior leaders had not included this incident in the log, no investigation had taken place, and no immediate mitigations were made to reduce further avoidable harm or to support clients. These concerns around the security of the premises from the neighbouring service were raised during our inspection in April 2025 and the provider outlined actions they planned to take by July 2025, but these had not been actioned.

Since our assessment in April 2025, the service had made improvements to the format of its incident log. However, it was still missing key sections, such as if a debrief was offered to clients and staff and any investigation details. The categories for incidents were not as clear as they could be, and several incidents were classed as ‘other’, which made analysis of themes harder. Since April 2025, the service had recorded 8 incidents. Of those, 2 were classed as ‘accident or illness requiring hospital treatment’, and 6 were classed as ‘other’. Three of these were related to falls, 1 was related to physical health concerns requiring hospital treatment, and 1 incident was related to security of the premises. We saw no evidence that staff and clients had received a verbal or written debrief following any incident. No incidents listed were noted to have had investigations, and there were no investigation reports available. We saw some evidence of lessons learned from certain incidents being discussed in team meeting minutes, but it was not clear what specific changes or improvements staff were required to make, or how the service would put in place mitigations to protect clients from further harm. This placed clients at risk of avoidable harm from identified risks in past incidents which were not responded to and mitigated against.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Medicines optimisation

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service did not ensure that medicines and treatments were safe and met people’s needs, capacities and preferences by enabling them to be involved in planning, including when changes happened.

During our assessment in April 2025, we found significant concerns under this quality statement. We served a warning notice around the safe management of medicines. During this assessment we did not see evidence of improvements and the warning notice had not been compiled with. We also found additional concerns during this inspection which we raised with the provider at the time. The warning notice outlined that we found evidence that staff were not all suitably trained in the provider's policy of medicines management, medicine errors were not comprehensively documented, thoroughly investigated, and actions were not taken to prevent future occurrence. It also outlined that leaders did not have oversight to ensure proper and safe management of medicines and did not manage identified risks appropriately.

The service had a medicines policy with processes for ordering, storing, administering and disposing of medication, but staff did not always follow this.

Medicines were not always administered in line with national guidance and legislation. During our assessment in April 2025, we identified incidents where staff had left medicines unattended in the presence of clients, which is not safe practice. During this current inspection, we saw this happen again. We observed one occasions where a nurse left medicines unattended with a client, and these were medicines belonging to another client. We observed two other administrations and saw that staff were not always consistent in following the correct procedure and checked the client’s name, their date of birth and allergies. For one client, the nurse only checked the client’s name. This was a concern as this client had a severe allergy.

The service did not always record client’s allergies on the administration record. Staff told us that the mitigation was that there are pictures of the clients on the system. However, we have concerns about the recording of allergies on the allergy tab since we saw that one client had a severe allergy, but this was not clear from the administration page.

Staff were provided with online medicines training, however there were no dates of completion or renewal, or levels of the qualification. No staff had their medicines competencies assessed following the last inspection. This was listed as an item on the provider’s action plan following our assessment in April 2025, but the registered manager confirmed this had not been done.

Despite the service medicines policy stating that clients could not self administer medicines using a dossete box (containers with separate compartments for days and times of the day, which can assist people with taking their medicines), we saw that one client had made up their own dosette box. We were told that the nurse had observed and supported this patient to make up this box from the original medicine’s packs, but there was no record of this. We could not find a risk assessment or care plan around this, and this did not follow the provider policy. This meant there was a risk that the client was not being appropriately supported to take their medicines safely and not all staff may have been aware of this arrangement or how to support this safely.

The service did not have an appropriate medicines lead, who was responsible for ensuring safe practice and reviewing and learning from medicines related incidents. Medicines errors were not thoroughly investigated, and actions were not taken to prevent a future occurrence.

Senior leaders had created and completed some medicines audits in line with the service’s policy. However, none of the senior leaders had a clinical background, leading to concerns around the effectiveness of these audits. The audits had not been completed consistently since our inspection in April 2025.

There was information available to staff in the nursing room on how to deal with emergencies. The service had access to emergency medicines and equipment such as Naloxone, EpiPens and defibrillators in case of emergency. They also had hypoglycaemia kits. However, glucose gels were found to be out of date. Staff could not clearly state who was responsible for checking these. Fortunately, there were no insulin dependent diabetics in the service so there was no immediate risk to people.

There were no identified issues with ordering or storing medicines. We saw that the service ensured that people had enough medicines. Medicines for disposal were segregated and sent back to the pharmacy. This was logged.

Medicines and controlled stationary were stored securely when not in use and the clinic room was clean and orderly. When prescriptions were written by the prescribing doctors, they were sent electronically to the pharmacy to be dispensed. A copy of the original prescription was posted or taken in by hand to the pharmacy when staff collected the medicine. Staff scanned and added the prescription to the client’s medical record. When private pink Controlled Drugs prescriptions were used by the prescribing doctors, the doctors kept their own records of their use including serials number of the prescriptions. The service did not have oversight of this.

We saw that information about care being delivered was routinely shared with people’s regular GP.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Safe and effective staffing

evidenceCategory.commentary:
At the inspection in April 2025, we found the service had a lack of oversight of several staffing areas. These included safe staff recruitment processes, staff training, staff supervision and appraisal. During this inspection, the service had taken limited action to address this, and concerns remained. Several areas of the service action plan had not been completed.

It remained the case that the service did not have a clear and accessible training matrix available for senior staff to know what training was required to be completed when, and by which staff. Information that was available did not clearly indicate when staff completed courses or when training was due for renewal. The service did not have a document outlining the minimum training requirements for staff. Staff had not received specific training that would support them in their role, such as supporting someone receiving care for substance misuse and managing mental health concerns in their service setting.

Although there was no clear supervision matrix for oversight of supervision taking place, staff told us they had supervision at regular intervals. We saw 2 supervision forms with headings guiding the supervisor in what to discuss.

The service had no vacancies. However, the service used a small number of agency nurses regularly. As we found in April 2025, we still saw no evidence to give assurances that they had received an appropriate induction and competency assessments. A folder was put together for one member of agency staff during our inspection.

In April 2025 we found that there were no competency assessments for staff duties appropriate to their role. As part of the service action plan, the service said each member of staff would have had their competency assessed for a range of areas by the end of June 2025. The information provided to us during the current inspection showed large gaps in the completion of these competency assessments. Staff acknowledged the positive work done by the quality lead in this area, but senior leaders had not planned the work effectively, to ensure it was completed by the deadline they had set.

The service had sufficient nursing and support staff to meet the needs of the clients. Managers had calculated the number of nurses and health care assistants required and the staffing establishment was complete, with 24- hour nursing in place.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Safe environments

evidenceCategory.commentary:
Since our assessment in April 2025, the service had made some changes to address concerns we identified. There were some areas that needed more work.

The service consisted of 6 single rooms and 2 double occupancy rooms, all with en-suite bathrooms. Clients had access to an outdoor space, a shared lounge, a dining area and meeting rooms. The garden was large, accessible and used for informal activities.

The service reviewed and improved its environmental risk assessment in May 2025. This now identified most hazard areas such as infection control, fire, falls, food safety and Control of Substances Hazardous to Health (COSHH), as well as areas that were missing in our April 2025 inspection, including mixed sex accommodation risks. The service had also assessed and put in place a ligatures risk assessment and installed a buzzer on the door from the garden. However, no action had been taken to assess the risk of using 70% alcohol-based hand gels that were available in communal areas. This may pose a risk for clients with addiction histories.

During this inspection we found some improvements with the management of products under COSHH. There was a secure, fire resistant, locked cupboard located in the staff office. We saw individual product sheets for items stored under COSHH.

Several concerns remained in place and insufficient action had been taken to address them. The service was still not secure from members of the public and the neighbouring service. Plans to install a fence between the services had not been carried out by the planned date, and no other mitigations had been put in place to address risks identified for clients in each service. There was no evidence that an action to create and implement a night-time security checklist had been done. Staff we spoke with did not know where to record risk assessments around the sharing of rooms.

During our April 2025 assessment, we found significant concerns around the management of fire safety and the service were non-compliant with the Fire Safety Order 2005. Since that assessment, the London Fire Brigade had inspected the service and systems to ensure they were in working order. Some areas for improvement in fire safety management remained, and had not been successfully embedded. Although there had been some checks recorded in the fire log book, these were inconsistent and it was unclear what needed to be checked and when. Fire assembly posters were located on the service walls, but they had not been completed with information on where the fire assembly point was located. There were no personal emergency evacuation plans (PEEPS) in place to support clients who would require support during an emergency evacuation, particularly those in the early stages of their detox regime.

Staff said they carried an alarm and radio they could use to alert colleagues to an emergency. Patients did not have access to an alarm to alert others to an emergency. A wall alarm system was fitted throughout the service in bedrooms and communal areas, but was not functioning.

The service had ligature cutters, but these were not in a clear and labelled location. During the inspection, the 3 members of staff asked to locate them, could not locate them easily. The ligature cutters did not have a designated location which was labelled clearly, which they should have done, to ensure staff knew where to get them in an emergency.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Safe systems, pathways and transitions

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service did not establish and maintain safe systems of care, in which safety is managed, monitored and assured. The service did not ensure continuity of care, including when people move between different services.

During our assessment in April 2025, we found concerns under this quality statement. These concerns remained during this assessment.

The service received referrals from self-funded clients. The service’s referral and admission process did not always ensure that essential information about the client was received and assessed to determine if the client’s needs could safely be met by the service. We saw records of 5 clients who had been admitted without their GP summary and examples where medicines had been prescribed without this GP summary being available. Some of these clients went on to have hospital admissions due to physical health deterioration. In the records we looked at, since April 2025, 3 clients were admitted to hospital with physical health complications during their care. For one of these clients, there was no pre-admission paperwork, no GP summary and no care plan or risk assessment available in the care records, prior to the incident. Clients were at risk of avoidable harm.

The service did not always follow its own inclusion and exclusion admissions criteria against each referral. We saw clients who had a history of seizures and uncontrolled diabetes admitted to the service, despite this meeting the exclusion criteria. There was no evidence of recognition or multidisciplinary discussion about this. We saw physical health complications and hospital admissions related to some of these patients.

The service did not involve the necessary healthcare and social care services to ensure patients had continuity of safe care both within the service and post discharge. We saw no evidence of professionals such as occupational therapists or community teams being involved in people’s care or discharge planning.

The service model of care remained unclear in some places. The standard operating procedure (SOP) had not been updated sufficiently following concerns raised about it during our April 2025 inspection. It still outlined that non-clinical staff would be involved in final decision making about admissions, which is outside of their clinical competency, and it did not clearly outline the reasons why something was listed as an exclusion criteria and could not be managed safely by the service.

The service had made some improvements to their policies and procedures. There were now policies relating to mixed sex accommodation, sexual safety, health and safety, fire safety and first aid. The service had also received assurances that staff had read and understood certain policies and procedures through read and sign sheets. However, key policies were still missing including whistleblowing; equality, diversity and inclusion; self-harm and suicide prevention; business continuity plan; training and development; and code of conducts for staff and clients.

As part of the action plan relating to the April 2025 inspection, the service planned to develop a new discharge policy, which would clearly outline how staff planned for and managed discharge, including any unplanned discharges. During this inspection, this documentation was not available and there was no evidence it had been created. There was also no evidence of discharge audits being developed and deployed, in line with this action plan. 7 of 9 client records we looked at did not include clear and detailed discharge planning information.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Safeguarding

evidenceCategory.commentary:
During our assessment in April 2025, we found concerns under this quality statement. These concerns remained during this assessment.

Most staff received training in safeguarding children and adults (Level 1 and 2). 6 of 9 staff had received training in safeguarding children and adults level 3.

In our April 2025 assessment, we found that staff had a lack of knowledge of safeguarding, including the identification of what is a safeguarding incident and safeguarding pathways throughout the service. To address this, the service planned to develop and carry out competency assessments in safeguarding to ensure they had appropriate knowledge for their role, by 30 May 2025. During this inspection, we found that these had taken place for three staff, but 6 remained outstanding.

There were safeguarding policies related to adults and children and evidence that staff had read or understood them, through a read and sign sheet. There were also safeguarding flowcharts to help staff follow the safeguarding pathway.

In April 2025, we found that the service had not made any safeguarding referrals to the local authority, despite there being a need to. During this inspection, we saw this had improved, and where staff had identified a safeguarding concern, this was referred to the local authority appropriately. Since our assessment in April 2025, the service had made one safeguarding referral to the local authority. The service had notified CQC of this referral.

Staff followed safe procedures for children visiting the service. No one under the age of 18 was allowed to visit the service.

Since the service registered in September 2024, there had been no incidents of restrictive interventions, including oral medicines, rapid tranquilisation, physical interventions or restraint.

In our April 2025 inspection, we found that information about some restrictions on clients using the service needed to be made clearer to clients. For example, that the front door of the service is locked and could only be opened by staff, and a clear list of any prohibited items shared. During this inspection, there was no evidence that the service had put in place actions it had outlined to address this. There was no signage to detail the restrictions in place or explanations to why, and we could not see evidence that restrictions or prohibited items were discussed with clients during their admission.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

keyQuestionRatings.name: Well-led
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
We looked for evidence that service leadership, management and governance assured high-quality, person-centred care; supported learning and innovation and promoted an open, fair culture.

This key question has been rated inadequate. This meant there were widespread and significant shortfalls in service leadership. Leaders and the culture they created did not assure the delivery of high-quality care. Leaders had not created supportive environments in which to work.

The concerns that we found in April 2025 had not been sufficiently addressed and remained in place. The senior leaders had failed to take action against the action plan they had put in place.

Leaders did not demonstrate the knowledge, skills and experience needed to deliver services effectively. Senior leaders did not have a clear understanding, oversight or proactive approach to an effective governance framework. There remained a lack of clear oversight and systems for safe admission, in ensuring appropriate information was available and appropriate staff were involved in final decision making. There remained lack of oversight of staff training, staff competence, poor audit practice, incident reporting and investigation.

topicareas.name: Capable, compassionate and inclusive leaders

evidenceCategory.commentary:
Leaders did not demonstrate the knowledge, skills and experience needed to deliver services effectively.

The service had four senior leaders which included three Directors; the Registered Manager, Nominated Individual and Company Director, and a Quality Assurance Consultant. Directors did not all have the appropriate qualifications, competence, skills and experience which were necessary for their role.

The senior staff had failed to deliver most actions on their action plan, which was put together to address concerns raised in April 2025. Despite being made aware of significant shortfalls, senior leaders had not taken appropriate action to address them. Shortfalls remained in multiple areas of fundamental standards. This included safe admission, safe care processes, discharge documentation, risk management, governance processes policies and procedures, fire safety, oversight of staff training, supervision and competence, and the management of incidents.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Freedom to speak up

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service did not create a positive culture where people feel that they can speak up and that their voice will be heard and information acted upon.

In April 2025 we found that there were insufficient policies or practice in place around to support staff to raise concerns about care. During this inspection, we found this had not been addressed effectively. The service did not have a whistleblowing policy in place, or equivalent. The service did not have a Freedom to Speak Up Guardian. The pathway for managing staff concerns was not documented well, clearly investigated, or evidenced that feedback was provided to staff about the outcome or lessons learned.

Staff said they felt able to speak up if something was not right. However, staff we spoke with said concerns they raised were not always responded to clearly or in a timely way. We saw no records of actions senior staff had taken in response to staff raising concerns.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Governance, management and sustainability

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service did not have clear responsibilities, roles, systems of accountability and good governance to manage and deliver good quality, sustainable care, treatment and support.

Our concerns from April 2025 remained in place. Senior leaders continued to demonstrate that they did not have a clear understanding of or oversight of effective governance systems for the service.

Regular governance meetings were not taking place. The process for reporting, reviewing, investigating and learning from incidents was not effective. Staff did not undertake appropriate audits to ensure safe and quality care was being provided and the senior leaders had not developed the suite of audits they outlined in their action plan. Examples of audits that had not been developed included weekly and monthly admissions audits, risk assessment audits, incident and complaints audits. Several checklists that the service planned to create had not been created in time with their own deadline. For example, an admissions checklist.

The service did not yet have a risk register. The service did not have a business continuity plan in place to cover eventualities such as adverse weather or a flu outbreak.

The systems and processes to oversee training compliance were not effective. Information did not clearly outline when training had taken place and when it was due to renewal. In one staff file, we saw they had completed over 20 training courses electronically in 1 day. This had not been identified by the service as an area for concern.

Senior leaders did not have sufficient access to information to support them with their management role. This included information on the performance of the service, staffing and client care.

The service had not made sufficient changes to the inclusion and exclusion criteria, to outline clearly why someone could not be cared for safely in that environment. As a result, the service had accepted referrals from some clients who were at risk of avoidable harm, due to the service not being able to safely meet their needs. In discussion with the senior managers, they acknowledged that some of these patients should not have been admitted.

The senior leaders planned to carry out a monthly governance audit, but this had only taken place once, on 30 May 2025.

There were several key policies still not available. These were related to whistleblowing; equality, diversity and inclusion; self-harm and suicide prevention; business continuity plan; The General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), confidentiality and data protection; training and development; and code of conducts for staff and clients.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Learning, improvement and innovation

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service did not have positive or well embedded practices around learning, innovation and improvement.

When incidents occurred, these were not always investigated. This meant no areas of learning were identified, were not shared with staff, and could not be embedded into the service to improve care.

Staff did not participate in national audits relevant to the service.

The service did not participate in accreditation schemes relevant to the service.

There was one quality improvement project in the service. This was around implementing the alternative to 12-step model approach to addiction.

The service had not managed to carry out several points within its action plan, to make improvements to the service.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Partnerships and communities

evidenceCategory.commentary: The service had not worked to gain a clear picture of the local services that it would engage with that could offer ongoing support to its clients. The service had not engaged services that may support clients with ongoing needs.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Shared direction and culture

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service did not have a shared vision, strategy and culture that is based on transparency, equity, equality and human rights, diversity and inclusion, engagement, and understanding and meeting the needs of people and communities.

There was no evidence to demonstrate how the senior leaders communicated their vision and strategy for the service to staff. Therapy staff were able to describe their approach and what was delivered to clients at the service. In general, staff did not have the opportunity to contribute to discussions about the strategy for the service.

During the inspection staff described a poor leadership culture and a lack of support from leaders. Leaders said they were present on site several times a week, but the signing in book indicated this was not the case.

A new general manager had started at the service two weeks before the inspection, but no information had been shared with them about the details of the previous inspection. The service action plan to address areas of concern had not been shared with them.

Staff told us they felt supported by the direct peers and enjoyed working with them. They said they often observed the clinical staff meeting the values of the service in their interactions with staff, and this was the case throughout our inspection.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Workforce equality, diversity and inclusion

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service did not clearly work towards an inclusive and fair culture by improving equality and equity for people who worked for them.

In April 2025, we found there were no key policies and procedures in place in relation to Equality, Diversity and Inclusion. There were no equality and diversity champions within the service e.g. LGBT+, BME etc. During this inspection, we did not see evidence that this had been addressed.

There remained no evidence about whether staff were able to apply to work flexibly e.g. flexible working agreements to account for personal circumstances such as caring responsibilities and health issues. We did not see evidence of managers putting reasonable adjustments in place for staff members to help them carry out their role.

overall.commentary:
We carried out an on-site assessment of TLC Rehab on 29 and 30 April 2026.

TLC Rehab registered with CQC in September 2024 to provide the regulated activities of Treatment of disease, disorder or injury and Accommodation for persons who require treatment for substance misuse. At the time of our inspection, the service did not have a Registered Manager. However, shortly after our assessment, the provider notified us of a new Registered Manager appointment.

We carried out a comprehensive assessment of all areas of the service. We also specifically reviewed the progress made against a warning notice served on the provider following an inspection in April 2025. This warning notice related to medicines management. The service had addressed the specific areas outlined in the warning notice.

Overall, we found that the service had made improvements in several areas. However, some risks remained and some areas needed further work.

We rated the service as requires improvement. We found breaches of regulations in relation to safe care and treatment, good governance, staffing and fit and proper persons employed.

We took enforcement action as a result of this assessment. We issued warning notices on 11 May 2026 in relation to safe care and treatment, staffing and fit and proper persons employed. The provider is required to become compliant with these warning notices by 20 July 2026.

For those areas where we found a need for improvement, but did not take enforcement action, we have asked the provider for an action plan. This action plan should outline how the provider intends to address the breaches identified and demonstrate sustained improvement.
