asgRatings.title: Ongoing Assessment for TLC Rehab
asgRatings.name: Residential substance misuse services
asgRatings.commentary:
Date of on-site assessment: 29 April – 30 April 2026. Further assessment activity, such as telephone calls with staff members and clients, took place up until 15 May 2026.

TLC Rehab is a residential substance misuse rehabilitation service for adults based in Barnet, north London. The service offers medically assisted detoxification treatment for alcohol, opiates and non-opiates. It is an independent service for self-funded clients, run by Apex Wellness Solutions Ltd.

TLC Rehab registered with CQC in September 2024 to provide the regulated activities of Treatment of disease, disorder or injury and Accommodation for persons who require treatment for substance misuse. At the time of our assessment, the service did not have a Registered Manager, although one was confirmed in post shortly after our assessment visit concluded.

The service offers mixed-sex accommodation for up to 10 people. At the time of our inspection, 7 clients were admitted to the service.

We carried out a short-term announced site visit on 29 and 30 April 2026 as part of a comprehensive assessment. This means we covered all key questions and quality statements. We have combined the scores for these to achieve the overall rating. We have rated the service as requires improvement.

This was our third inspection of this service. During our initial assessment in April 2025, we found serious concerns and multiple breaches of regulations. We took urgent enforcement action and issued a Section 31 Letter of Intent relating to a range of governance and safety issues. At that time, we also issued a warning notice relating to medicines management. During our second assessment in July 2025, the provider was unable to demonstrate sufficient progress in addressing the areas of concern. The issues within the warning notice had not been addressed and the warning notice remained in place. As a result of the assessment in July 2025, we took urgent enforcement action by imposing conditions on the provider’s registration. At both previous assessments, we rated the service inadequate.

We undertook this current assessment to check whether the issues in the warning notice had been addressed and what progress the provider had made in improving overall governance and safety. We found that several areas had improved, but some risks remained and some areas needed further embedding.

At this current inspection, we found that the provider was in breach of regulations in relation to safe care and treatment, good governance, staffing, and fit and proper persons employed:

  • Regulation 12: Safe care and treatment. Staff did not always provide safe care and treatment in line with national guidance. Medicines were not always prescribed safely. The provider had not ensured that its prescriber liaised with clients’ GPs consistently to make sure that care and treatment remained safe. Potential risks to people using the service were not identified, assessed and mitigated where needed. The provider had not ensured that staff had followed its policy for admissions to the service. This meant that the service was not able to meet the needs of all clients safely. Not all safety incidents were documented and investigated appropriately.
  • Regulation 17: Good governance. There was no clinical lead role within the service to oversee and drive continuous improvement and provide expert guidance to the team. Decisions about some client admissions had been made by a non-clinical staff member, resulting in inappropriate admissions.
  • Regulation 18: Staffing. Nurses did not receive appropriate clinical supervision or continuing professional development. There was no written contract for the employment of doctors and no contingency arrangements for continuity of care during their absences.
  • Regulation 19: Fit and proper persons employed. The provider had not established a process to check that all staff it employed were of good character and had the necessary qualifications, competence, skills and experience, or were registered with the relevant professional body where such registration was required.

We took enforcement action as a result of this inspection. We issued warning notices on 11 May 2026 in relation to safe care and treatment, staffing, and fit and proper persons employed. The provider is required to become compliant with these warning notices by 20 July 2026.

We also found other areas where practice needed improving. We saw some gaps in clients’ assessments, such as previous treatment history not being explored and the absence of relevant blood tests. It was not always clear whether clients had been assessed by the doctor remotely or face-to-face, in line with the provider’s policy. There was limited evidence of harm reduction advice being provided to clients. Fire evacuation drills had not been carried out since March 2025. Although overall compliance with training was between 75% and 95%, this varied for individual staff members and some training courses. The Oliver McGowan mandatory training on learning disability and autism was included in the provider’s optional training instead of mandatory training. Actions identified in the external health and safety review in January 2026 remained outstanding. The service did not routinely work with external organisations and did not participate in research, quality improvement or accreditation schemes.

We found several areas where improvements had been made since our last assessment. Clients’ recovery plans that we viewed were personalised, holistic and recovery-oriented, with evidence of client involvement. We saw tangible improvements in the service’s governance systems and in how staff used them. The service had improved its systems to manage environmental risks. This included improved fire safety management, having a risk register and business continuity plan in place, and improvements to the security of the premises. The new operational managers demonstrated a good understanding and oversight of the service. Staff said that the improvements in governance helped them in performing their roles. Staff meeting structure had improved and weekly community meetings were taking place. There were now appropriate policies and procedures in place, including clear inclusion and exclusion criteria for admissions to the service. Discharge planning process had improved. The service had implemented a range of audits to monitor the quality and safety of the service. The service now ensured that staff received competency assessments, training, managerial supervision and appraisal. The service collected data such as outcome measures to monitor how effective the service was. Managers had access to information needed to support them in their role, such as audits, performance and staffing data.
asgRatings.narrative: The service is not performing as well as it should and we have told the service how it must improve.
asgRatings.overallPeopleExperience:
We spoke with 5 clients and attended a weekly community meeting. We also spoke with 2 clients who were recently discharged from the service. Client feedback was mixed.

Most clients reported feeling safe at the service. However, some clients had raised concerns about a peer’s behaviour and said no action had been taken by the service to address concerns when they had raised them.

Clients described some staff as kind, caring and friendly, but said this was not consistent across all staff. Some clients told us their care was less individualised than they had expected, or not in line with what they had read about the service prior to their admission. Some clients reported difficulties in accessing the prescriber to discuss their treatment plan. Clients gave mixed feedback about how well their medicines were managed and described experiencing some disorganisation or lack of knowledge around their medicine administration.

We saw that clients were confident to raise issues that concerned them in the community meeting we observed. Clients knew how to complain if needed.

Some clients reported dissatisfaction with the standard of cleaning within the service. We heard that maintenance issues were generally addressed but this could take some time.

We heard very positive feedback about one-to-one therapy, the service’s chef and the weekly running club. However, some clients found the therapeutic style of some group facilitators inconsistent and said that yoga and daily walk did not always happen.

Two recently discharged clients told us their needs were met well at the service and that they were happy with the aftercare support they received.

The service collected feedback from clients after their treatment was completed. The results from November 2025 showed that most people rated it as good or outstanding.

keyQuestionRatings.name: Caring
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
This means we looked for evidence that the service involved people and treated them with compassion, kindness, dignity and respect.

At our last assessment we rated this key question requires improvement. At this assessment the rating has remained requires improvement.

This meant people did not always feel well-supported, cared for or treated with dignity and respect.
keyQuestionRatings.narrative: This service is not always caring

topicareas.name: Independence, choice and control

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service informed people of their rights and involved them in conversations and decisions about their care.

The service received referrals from people who self-referred. Staff clearly documented clients’ choices in relation to consent and information sharing.

Recovery plans we viewed were personalised, holistic and recovery-oriented, with evidence of client involvement. In all records staff documented that the client had been offered a copy of their plan.

Clients told us that therapy staff had recommended specific additional reading materials that had been useful to them and their own treatment and care.

The service had now improved its discharge planning process. For example, a recently discharged client said staff supported them to build their own aftercare and involved them in this process.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Kindness, compassion and dignity

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The clients’ feedback on how staff engaged with them was mostly positive, but there were examples where this could be improved.

Clients’ feedback about staff was mixed. They said some staff were kind, caring, and friendly, but this was not consistent across the whole staff group. Clients said some staff really cared and would do anything to help, describing them as “amazing”. However, we were told about 2 examples where clients said that the response from staff when raising an issue was dismissive. One client said a staff member had shared personal information about their peer, which did not feel appropriate to them.

During our visit, we observed staff engaging with clients in a relaxed, supportive, and respectful manner. Most staff we spoke with discussed clients with kindness and compassion and demonstrated they knew them well. However, one member of staff demonstrated a less compassionate attitude by using stigmatising language when describing the client group they supported.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Responding to people’s immediate needs

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service did not always understand and listen to people’s needs, views and wishes. Staff did not always respond to people’s needs in the moment or act to minimise any discomfort, concern, or distress.

Some clients shared concerns about inappropriate or disruptive comments and behaviour from another client. They told us they had raised this with staff, but this had not been effectively addressed. Clients described the negative impact this had on their own experience.

In the week before our inspection, staff had been unable to get in contact with the manager on call one evening, to seek support and resource to manage client dissatisfaction with a meal made by an agency chef. This had resulted in 1 client purchasing a takeaway meal for themselves and several others with their own money. Clients said management staff had not responded well in the moment, or afterwards, to support clients around the impact of this.

However, clients we spoke with told us they felt safe at the service. Clients could raise their concerns at weekly community meetings and reported issues such as maintenance. They said these were addressed, although sometimes after one week, rather than immediately.

Staff discussed changing risks to, or posed by, clients in daily meetings. During our visit, we saw staff engaging with clients and responding to their requests promptly.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Treating people as individuals

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service treated people as individuals and aimed to ensure people’s care, support, and treatment met their needs and preferences. They took account of people’s strengths, abilities, aspirations, culture and unique backgrounds and protected characteristics.

Staff provided clients with a comprehensive welcome pack with information on treatments, local services, their rights, advocacy organisations, and how to complain.

Staff knew about communication needs of people with protected characteristics under the Equality Act 2010, and 80% had completed the Oliver McGowan mandatory training on learning disabilities and autism.

Clients were provided with a choice of food to meet their dietary needs, intolerances, or preferences. On admission, each client completed a form to inform the chef of any allergies, likes, and dislikes. This was displayed clearly in the kitchen, and clients said the chef always adhered to this. Clients said that the chef was “brilliant” and always wanted feedback on individual preferences. The chef joined the weekly community meetings to gather feedback on the planned menu, any changes, and meal plans. A nutritionist visited the service weekly, which the clients described positively.

We did not see information on display to make diverse groups of people feel welcome and included. For example, those from LGBTQ+ communities or other minoritised groups.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Workforce wellbeing and enablement

evidenceCategory.commentary:
Whilst staff were largely positive about working in the service, the lack of clinical leadership in the service meant that staff could not always access the support needed in a timely manner to undertake their roles.

Due to an absence of clinical leadership within the service, the nurses employed by the service did not receive appropriate clinical supervision or supported professional development to enable them to perform their roles to the best of their abilities.

The service had commissioned an external review around health and safety compliance relating to staff employment which pointed out several areas that had not been completed. These areas were recommended in line with good practice. Examples of areas recommended for completion were health assessments for employees who work overnight and display screen equipment risk assessments.

Staff we spoke with said they were happy to work for the service. Several staff said they were proud of supporting clients.

Staff said IT was sufficient to carry out their roles and was not a barrier.

The service monitored staff sickness and absence rates. Staff sickness absence in the 6 months prior to our inspection was 6 days.

Staff received annual appraisals. Appraisals included conversations about personal strengths and objectives.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

keyQuestionRatings.name: Effective
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
This means we looked for evidence that people’s care, treatment and support achieved good outcomes and promoted a good quality of life, based on best available evidence.

At our last assessment we rated this key question requires improvement. At this assessment the rating has remained requires improvement.

This meant the effectiveness of people’s care, treatment and support did not always achieve good outcomes or was inconsistent.
keyQuestionRatings.narrative: This service is not always effective

topicareas.name: Assessing needs

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service did not always make sure people’s care and treatment were effective because they did not always check and discuss people’s health, care, wellbeing and communication needs with them.

We reviewed 4 care and treatment records and found that comprehensive assessments of substance use had not been completed for every client. In 3 records staff had not explored clients’ previous treatment history. There was no evidence of assessing any of the clients’ blood borne virus (BBV) status. For 2 clients admitted for alcohol treatment, there was no evidence of relevant blood tests such as liver function tests being obtained prior to admission, despite one of these clients reporting that they had liver cirrhosis. For one client, staff had made an initial assessment of their needs, but had not identified or acted upon the impact of their inappropriate behaviour on other clients. Several clients told us it made them uncomfortable and impacted their own experience of the service, but this had not been managed appropriately by the service.

The service used a global risk stratification tool for client risk assessments, rating the risk as low, medium or high overall and assigning the frequency of review accordingly. This included individuals who were at risk of suicide or deliberate self-harm. This was not in line with national guidance, which advises not to use risk stratification to predict future suicide or the repetition of self-harm.

The admission policy stipulated the criteria for when clients must be assessed face-to-face prior to admission. In 1 care record it was not clear if the client had been assessed remotely or face-to-face because staff recorded both options in the assessment form. There was limited evidence of a full physical health assessment on admission in the care records we viewed.

Since our last inspection in July 2025, we saw improvement in staff considering whether the service could safely meet a person’s needs. The service had declined a number of referrals due to recognising they could not safely meet those clients’ needs. The service referred clients to more appropriate care where possible. For example, 2 people were referred to the emergency department at a local acute hospital. However, during our assessment, we saw 2 clients had still been admitted to the service despite meeting its exclusion criteria. This remained an area for the service to address.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Consent to care and treatment

evidenceCategory.commentary:
Whilst the service had trained staff to apply the Mental Capacity Act, there were concerns about its use in practice in the service.

In the care records we reviewed, we saw evidence that staff had assessed clients’ mental capacity and documented consent, confidentiality, and information sharing.

Compliance with Mental Capacity Act training was 80%. However, only 60% of staff had completed training in consent for health and social care.

One client was assessed as having the capacity to decide on admission to the service, but their capacity to make other ongoing specific decisions was queried by some staff. We heard concerns from staff and other clients that the needs of this client exceeded those that the service was able to support safely. We raised this as an area for the service to address immediately during our assessment.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Delivering evidence-based care and treatment

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service did not always plan and deliver people’s care and treatment with them, including what was important and mattered to them.

The service offered care and treatment interventions suitable for the client group. These were medically assisted detoxification treatment for alcohol, opiates and non-opiates, and psychosocial interventions which included group and individual therapy. The interventions were those recommended by guidance from the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE).

Feedback from most clients about the one-to-one therapy sessions was very positive. They described staff delivering these and impact of the sessions as ‘amazing’. However, 3 clients said the difference in therapeutic style of the staff delivering group work caused some confusion and lack of consistency across the groups and one-to-one sessions. Managers we spoke with acknowledged the limitations of the current therapy programme and told us about plans to improve it.

The service had now developed and implemented a range of clinical audits. These included audits of care records, admissions, incidents, concerns and complaints, health and safety compliance, food safety, discharge planning, medical equipment and medicine management. These audits identified actions that were linked to an action plan and marked as completed in the audits we looked at. The service had commissioned a full service audit in November 2025. However, due to the ongoing lack of clinical leadership, there were limitations to how the service could use the results of clinical audits to measure and improve the effectiveness of the treatments it provided.

In most care records we viewed, there was limited evidence of regular medical and prescribing reviews.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: How staff, teams and services work together

evidenceCategory.commentary:
Whilst internal meetings had improved, some were still not taking place regularly or with the correct attendees.

The service held daily flash meetings and monthly team meetings, although monthly meetings had not taken place every month due to the recent high staff turnover. We observed a flash meeting where staff discussed and shared information about each client effectively. There were also managerial and clinical governance meetings. Managers explained that the previous plan to hold fortnightly meetings had not worked due to the relatively small team size. Meetings were now minuted and minutes were available to staff on a shared drive.

The doctors working for the service did not routinely attend team meetings. This limited information sharing and discussions about patient care and clinical decisions.

The service did not regularly work with external teams or organisations.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Monitoring and improving outcomes

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service routinely used outcome measures to monitor people’s progress.

We reviewed 4 care and treatment records and saw evidence that staff used recognised rating scales, such as the Alcohol use disorders identification test consumption (AUDIT-C) and the Severity of Alcohol Dependence Questionnaire (SADQ).

The service had now started monitoring client outcomes. We viewed a quarterly audit of outcome measures including the World Health Organisation Wellbeing Index (WHO-5), the generalised anxiety disorder assessment (GAD-7), depression assessment (PHQ-9), length of stay and treatment goals. The service had identified an area for improvement which was to ensure higher compliance with completing outcome measures on discharge.

A lack of clinical leadership limited the service’s ability to use data from outcome measures to monitor treatments and drive continuous improvement.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Supporting people to live healthier lives

evidenceCategory.commentary:
Whilst clients were offered healthy food and some activities, the service did not always actively support people to live healthier lives, or where possible, reduce their future needs for care and support.

Sessions that were on an activity timetable were not taking place regularly. This included a weekly yoga class and a daily walking group. Clients told us the yoga teacher had not attended in several weeks and the daily walk did not take place. They said this would be valued. Clients and some staff said that the physical exercise on offer was limited and thought that clients would benefit from more physical activity.

The care records we reviewed showed that limited harm reduction advice was provided to clients. Staff did not check clients’ blood borne virus (BBV) status and did not always request relevant blood tests for clients whose liver may have been damaged by alcohol use.

The service did not offer clear smoking cessation schemes. The rules and procedures around staff smoking were not clearly available for staff or clients. We were told that 2 clients had increased their smoking or started smoking whilst at the service. The service did not have a clear policy for staff smoking at the workplace, including where this could or could not take place.

The service had a large garden that clients could access at any time. There was seating available for people who wanted to spend time outside.

The service offered a table tennis table in the garden for clients to use. A staff member recently organised a weekly running club for clients who wished to join in. Clients who had attended gave very positive feedback about the benefits.

The service employed a chef to prepare fresh food on site. Clients’ feedback about the chef was extremely positive. The chef recently started making ginger energy shots for clients to support their health and wellbeing. The chef planned healthy meals and adapted these to the needs and preferences of clients.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

keyQuestionRatings.name: Responsive
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
This means we looked for evidence that the service met people’s needs.

At our last assessment we rated this key question requires improvement. At this assessment the rating has changed to good.

This meant people’s needs were met through good organisation and delivery.

topicareas.name: Care provision, Integration and continuity

evidenceCategory.commentary:
Clients were supported to maintain contact with family and friends and participate in community-based activities.

Staff supported clients to maintain contact with their families and carers in line with their wishes. One client told us about their friend supporting them through assessment and how staff included the friend in this process. Clients could keep their phones and laptops during admission.

Staff supported clients to access education or work opportunities when relevant. For example, a client told us that a healthcare assistant had supported them to update their CV to make steps to getting back into work and described this as extremely helpful.

Staff ensured that clients could access appropriate spiritual support. Spiritual needs were explored on admission. Staff told us that support workers could accompany clients to their chosen place of worship.

A client who was recently discharged told us they were given a plan and information on community support available.

The service had not established links with organisations or specialist providers in the local area that might support development of this even more.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Equity in access

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service made sure that people with protected characteristics such as a physical disability, could access the care, support and treatment they needed when they needed it.

The service was equipped with a lift, and accommodation on the ground floor was available for people who had mobility needs. The lift was in working order at the time of our inspection. The service made it clear during assessment if they could not accommodate someone’s physical disability needs in their environment.

The service had a form to complete personal emergency evacuation plans (PEEPs) for any clients requiring assistance during evacuations. No PEEPs were in place at the time of our inspection. Following our feedback, managers provided assurance that these would be put in place going forward.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Equity in experiences and outcomes

evidenceCategory.commentary:
Staff and leaders actively listened to information about people who are most likely to experience inequality in experience or outcomes and tailored their care, support and treatment in response to this.

The service had now ensured that staff received mandatory training in equality, diversity and human rights, and 94% of staff had completed it. Additionally, 80% of staff had completed the Oliver McGowan mandatory training on learning disabilities and autism. Staff we spoke with thought the service was inclusive of diverse groups of people, including those with protected characteristics under the Equality Act 2010.

Clients we spoke with did not raise any concerns about discrimination.

There was no information on display to make groups with protected characteristics feel welcome and included, which would promote a positive approach to equality and inclusion.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Listening to and involving people

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service made it easy for people to share feedback and ideas, or raise complaints about their care, treatment and support. They involved people in decisions about their care and told them what had changed as a result.

The service had clear information available about how to raise a concern or make a formal complaint, including to external bodies. Clients we spoke with confirmed they knew how to complain if needed. The service carried out a monthly review of concerns and complaints to ensure compliance with the complaints handling policy. The service had received 4 complaints and 2 informal concerns in the 6 months before our inspection.

Staff knew how to handle complaints appropriately and received feedback on the outcomes of investigations as needed. We saw learning identified from complaints. For example, specific additional training was given to staff following a complaint. Following recent complaints about the poor quality of food prepared by agency staff, the service was recruiting a part-time chef to cover the weekends.

The service held weekly community meetings where clients were asked for feedback about care, both to share positive experiences and raise any concerns or maintenance issues. In the community meeting we attended, clients were confident to raise issues that concerned them.

The service also monitored compliments received and shared these with staff. From the audits we saw that 7 compliments were received between November 2025 and March 2026.

The service collected feedback from clients after treatment was completed. Information from an audit in November 2025 showed that 4 of 8 clients rated the service as outstanding in all areas, and others rated it as outstanding or good.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Person-centred Care

evidenceCategory.commentary:
Whilst clients had individual recovery plans in place, the service delivered did not always meet people’s individual needs.

Although the care records demonstrated that most clients’ recovery plans were personalised and holistic, we heard some mixed feedback from clients. Some clients reported having limited access to the prescriber, meaning they could not always discuss their treatment plan and request changes to it.

Two clients said there were some maintenance issues that would make their stay more comfortable, if addressed. For example, some rugs looked worn and should be cleaned or replaced. One client did not have a desk available in their bedroom on admission, and another did not have a bedside lamp. The service did not provide terrestrial TV, and clients were required to use their own subscription services if they wanted to use the TV in their bedroom.

Two recently discharged clients told us their individual needs were met well at the service. However, 2 current clients told us they were disappointed with the service delivered and expected to receive more individualised care. Two clients said some of the group sessions felt more tailored to people getting support for alcohol detoxification, rather than other substances.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Planning for the future

evidenceCategory.commentary:
People were supported to plan for important life changes, so they could have enough time to make informed decisions about their future.

We saw evidence that the service had now improved its discharge planning process, including planning for an unexpected treatment exit. Two former clients we spoke with were positive about their discharge plan and the aftercare support they received. A client who was discharged during our inspection visit was prescribed appropriate relapse prevention medications. Staff told us they provided clients with harm minimisation advice and Naloxone (a life-saving medication used to rapidly reverse an opioid overdose) if they were at risk of experiencing an overdose on discharge.

The standard aftercare offer consisted of 3 follow-up calls with a therapist and weekly online meetings. Leaders told us about plans to improve this provision further.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Providing Information

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service provided a welcome pack, but did not always supply appropriate, accurate, and up-to-date information on its website or within the premises.

Staff provided clients with a comprehensive welcome pack which included information on treatments, local services that the public could access, their rights, advocacy organisations, complaints, safety arrangements, and restrictions within the service.

However, some clients told us the care they received was not in line with their expectations from what they read about the service prior to their admission. Two clients were concerned that the service’s most recent CQC rating was not clearly displayed and said they would not have come to the service had they known it. We were told that the ratings poster on the premises was previously not visible as it was obscured by other information on the notice board. At the time of our inspection, the provider had not reflected the CQC rating on its website. We raised this with the managers during our visit, and they took prompt action to make the rating clearly visible. Registered providers must ensure their ratings are displayed conspicuously and legibly at each location and on their website.

Staff and managers had access to information to support them in their role. For example, meeting minutes were now available to staff to read. However, while community meeting minutes were available to staff, they were not shared with clients. We discussed this with managers, who said they would make them available on the information board.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

keyQuestionRatings.name: Safe
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
This means we looked for evidence that people were protected from abuse and avoidable harm.

At our last assessment we rated this key question inadequate. At this assessment the rating has changed to requires improvement.

This meant some aspects of the service were not always safe and there was limited assurance about safety. There was an increased risk that people could be harmed.

The service was in breach of regulations in relation to safe care and treatment, staffing, and fit and proper persons employed.
keyQuestionRatings.narrative: This service is not always safe

topicareas.name: Infection prevention and control

evidenceCategory.commentary:
Whilst there had been improvements from the previous inspection, the service did not always keep shared spaces as clean as they should be.

During our visit, the care environment appeared mostly clean and well-maintained.

All staff had completed the mandatory infection and prevention control (IPC) training. The service carried out a food safety audit, showing an increase in compliance from 81% in October 2025 to over 96% in 2026. However, food safety training completion was 60%.

The service employed an external contractor to carry out daily cleaning. Cleaning records we viewed were up to date and demonstrated that all areas were cleaned regularly. However, some clients we spoke with reported dissatisfaction with the standard of cleaning within the service. Clients said there had been occasions when cleaning of shared spaces was not always thorough, for example used tissues being left on the ground for 3 days. One client said they would have preferred personal spaces, such as bathrooms and bedrooms, to be cleaned more regularly.

Staff carried out other appropriate checks to detect and prevent the spread of infections. A Legionella risk assessment had been carried out, and regular monitoring of the water systems took place.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Involving people to manage risks

evidenceCategory.commentary:
Whilst the service had systems in place to assess and manage individual risk, they did not always work well with people to understand and manage risks. They did not always provide care to meet people’s needs that was safe, supportive and enabled them to do the things that mattered to them.

We reviewed 4 care and treatment records. All contained risk assessments and risk management plans, although these were not always up to date or covered every area of risk comprehensively. In 3 records, we saw management plans were kept up-to-date, but for 1 client there was no evidence of updates to their risk management following incidents that had been reported. Three records included plans for an unexpected treatment exit.

Most clients we spoke with reported feeling safe at the service. Clients could raise their concerns at weekly community meetings. However, some clients shared concerns about inappropriate behaviour from a peer which they had raised with managers but this had not led to change. This was impacting their experience at the service.

Three clients told us that staff did not always carry out searches of bags when returning to the service from visiting the local area, in line with provider policy. Staff did not always carry these searches out immediately at the time of return, which they should have done. This created opportunities for items to be brought into the service without staff knowledge. Clients raised this as an area of concern, which we fed back to the service on the day of the assessment. The service said they would be addressed immediately, through discussions with staff and reinforcement of the importance of these searches.

Staff involved patients in care planning and risk assessment. There was evidence of personalised planning and client voice in the records we viewed.

Staff we spoke with were aware of the risks specific to the client group they supported. Most staff were trained in administering Naloxone (a life-saving medication to rapidly reverse an opioid overdose), immediate life support, management of seizures and anaphylaxis awareness. Approximately 75% of eligible staff had been trained in completing observations.

The client welcome pack outlined the arrangements for safety and security within the service and provided details of emergency helplines.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Learning culture

evidenceCategory.commentary:
Whilst the service had systems in place to report and respond to incidents, they did not always have a proactive and positive culture of safety based on openness and honesty. They did not always listen to concerns about safety and did not always investigate and report safety events. Lessons were not always learnt to continually identify and embed good practice.

The service used an incident recording system that all staff could access. In addition, staff were required to detail incidents within each client’s care record. Managers received alerts when new incidents were reported.

When staff did report incidents, the incident reporting system was effective in supporting review by a manager, capturing detailed information about the incident and a section for learning.

Although we found that staff reported some incidents, staff did not identify and report all incidents. We identified 2 incidents that staff had not reported which could have led to potential harm and required review and actions to reduce the chance of them happening again.

In most incident records we viewed, we saw appropriate learning and action as a result of staff review and discussion. However, for 1 incident that involved a client and staff member, we did not. This area required further strengthening to ensure that risk of avoidable harm identified from past incidents was responded to and mitigated against to prevent future recurrence. We saw that staff did not update the client’s risk management plan, which would have meant further risks relating to their behaviour could have been mitigated more effectively. There was no evidence that a debrief was offered to staff or the client.

We saw evidence of improvements made based on learning from previous incidents. This process had improved since our last inspection, but needed to be better embedded to be fully effective. We reviewed staff meeting minutes for March 2026 and saw limited evidence of discussions about incidents and learning. Staff we spoke with were able to share limited examples of recent learning from incidents.

The duty of candour is a statutory duty that requires registered providers to act in an open and transparent way with people receiving care or treatment and includes specific requirements for certain notifiable safety incidents. Duty of candour was part of staff training and 75% of staff had completed it.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Medicines optimisation

evidenceCategory.commentary:
Whilst we found that the service had addressed areas of concern relating to training and documentation from a previous inspection, during this inspection we identified concerns relating to safe practice. We did see that medicines were stored appropriately.

At our initial assessment in April 2025, we found serious concerns relating to medicines management. We took enforcement action and issued a warning notice. At that time, staff had not been suitably trained in the provider’s medicines management policy, medicines errors were not documented appropriately, and leaders did not have oversight of medicines management. During our assessment in July 2025, we found the provider had not demonstrated sufficient progress in addressing the issues within the warning notice. At this current assessment, the provider had demonstrated adequate improvement in these areas and was now compliant with the specific concerns outlined in the warning notice. Staff received appropriate training in the provider’s medicines management policy and reported medicines errors appropriately.

During the current assessment we found several areas that needed improving to ensure safe and effective practice. We saw examples where assessments and prescribing had not taken place in line with best practice guidance or the provider’s own policy. Two clients were admitted to the service without evidence that the service had attempted to request a summary from the GP to verify their medical history. One of these clients had a new medicine prescribed. The provider’s policy stated that staff should do all they can to obtain a GP summary upon admission. Not having information from the GP meant that all healthcare professionals involved in clients’ care were not aware of their changing physical health needs and potential drug interactions. For one person, a new medicine was initiated due to an elevated blood pressure reading. However, it was unclear from the notes whether the client was already taking medicines for this, whether the blood pressure was persistently elevated and whether prescribing for physical health fell within the provider’s remit.

Another client was prescribed a medicine for an unlicensed indication, or outside the product licences, known as ‘off label’ use. There was no clear rationale for this prescribing decision and no evidence of informed consent from the client documented in the care record, which was not in line with national guidance.

Most consultations were done remotely, and we found evidence that some prescribing took place without a consultation, with information and symptom management being relayed between a client and remote prescriber by a staff nurse.

Clients we spoke with gave mixed feedback about how their medicines were managed. For example, 2 clients described several occasions when staff had not been clear about what time specific medicines were to be administered, causing confusion both for clients and nursing staff. One client said they had different information from different staff about the medicines they were receiving.

We did find that the service had made several improvements in the governance arrangements around medicines since our last inspection. Management staff now carried out medicines management and medical equipment audits, including ensuring medicines errors were reported. These highlighted areas for improvement or non-compliance with provider policy. However, it was not clear who took a lead role in embedding improved clinical practice based on the audit outcomes, as there was no clinical lead role for the service. A separate, one-off audit conducted in December 2025 highlighted some issues in relation to the treatment room. The findings of the audit were not shared or acted on. Managers advised they were not aware of the audit, and the staff member responsible had since left. During our assessment, we did not see evidence of any clinical or prescribing audits.

We saw that medicines were stored appropriately. Medicines prescribed for clients (their own medicines as well as those prescribed by the provider) were stored in a locked cupboard. The keys were kept with the nurse on duty. Each client had their own clearly labelled container. Controlled drugs (CDs) were stored in a separate cupboard. A CD register was kept and checked daily. A random CD check showed no discrepancies. An emergency medicines kit and emergency equipment were available on site.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Safe and effective staffing

evidenceCategory.commentary:
During our previous inspections we identified concerns around safe recruitment processes, staff training, supervision and appraisal. At this inspection, although we saw some improvements in this area, ongoing concerns remained. There was no clinical lead in place, which was impacting several other areas of ensuring safe and effective practice.

We were concerned that despite providing medically assisted treatment, the service had no clinical leadership role in place. Although the service engaged the services of 2 doctors, this arrangement was informal, with no written contract for their employment. The doctors provided assessment and prescribing input, but were not employed in a clinical lead role. A clinical lead provides clear clinical leadership (guiding, influencing, and improving clinical practice to deliver safe, effective, and high-quality patient care), ensures consistent quality of care, supports staff development and coordinates service delivery effectively across the team.

There were no arrangements for clinical supervision or audits to ensure that clinical practice adhered to best practice guidance. The service had briefly employed a lead nurse, who recently left this role and there were no plans to replace them. The nurses employed by the service did not receive clinical supervision or professional development to enable them to carry out the duties they were employed to perform within the service. There was no oversight of the doctors’ prescribing. This meant that the provider had failed to determine and review the appropriate leadership requirements and staff supervision needs required to safely meet the needs of clients.

The service had not established or followed safer recruitment processes. For one staff member, we saw no evidence of a risk assessment required in line with safe recruitment practice. The need for this had not been considered in the provider’s safer recruitment policy. For another staff member, there was a lack of evidence to clearly demonstrate their right to work in the UK. There was no documentation available on the doctors working for the service such as proof of identity, satisfactory evidence of conduct in previous employment, evidence of continued professional registration or appropriate indemnity cover.

It was not clear what contingency arrangements were in place for continuity of care during planned or unplanned absences of the main assessing and prescribing doctor. Some of the clients we spoke with told us they had not met the doctor face-to-face, and some said they found it difficult to speak with the doctor when needed.

Compliance with training was between 75% and 95% overall. However, this varied for individual members of staff. For example, 2 staff members had not completed any of the training assigned to them that the provider described as continuing professional development (CPD) training. There was no evidence of mandatory training completion for the doctors working at the service. Although 80% of staff had completed the Oliver McGowan mandatory training on learning disability and autism, this training was listed as part of the provider’s CPD instead of mandatory training. The Health and Care Act 2022 introduced a statutory requirement that registered providers must ensure their staff receive this training.

New staff now completed a structured induction programme. We spoke with a new member of staff who confirmed that their induction was ongoing. However, records showed that week 1 and month 1 induction checks were outstanding for 2 employees, although their day 1 and month 6 induction checks had been marked as complete.

The service had seen high staff turnover at 36% in the 6 months before our inspection. During our visit, the service was fully staffed. Two new operational leaders were recently appointed as the Registered Manager and Nominated Individual, both of whom were knowledgeable and appropriately experienced.

There were sufficient nursing and support staff to meet the needs of the clients. The team was a combination of directly employed staff and independent practitioners. It included nurses, doctors, healthcare assistants, recovery workers, therapists and managers. A self-employed nutritionist visited the service once a week.

Since our last inspection we saw there had been improvements in some areas. The service now had arrangements to monitor that staff received competency assessments, training, supervision and appraisal. Competency assessment audits demonstrated improvement in compliance from 58% in November 2025 to 100% in February 2026.

Compliance with quarterly managerial supervision was 90% in February 2026 and appraisals had been completed by all eligible staff (6 in total).

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Safe environments

evidenceCategory.commentary:
Although we saw a significant improvement in how the service detected and controlled potential risks in the care environment since our last inspection, there were a small number of areas that still needed addressing.

Two areas of improvement were needed in the management of a safe environment. The service had a health and safety review by an external provider in January 2026 which identified actions for completion. There was no evidence of their completion and these actions remained outstanding at the time of our inspection. Staff had not carried out any fire evacuation drills since March 2025. This meant that staff familiarity with emergency evacuation procedures, which is routinely developed through regular fire drills, may be limited.

Overall, however, we saw improved systems to manage fire safety. The service had appropriate policies and procedures in place. Essential fire safety information was included in the client welcome pack. There were information boards for clients, staff and visitors in communal spaces about what to do in an emergency, giving clear instruction for fire assembly points. Fire assembly points were clearly signposted in areas outside of the building. The service carried out monthly fire safety audits. We saw that these were completed for the 6 months leading up to our inspection, with compliance rates over 95%. A fire risk assessment was in place and the necessary checks were completed regularly, with records kept. Compliance with fire safety training was 100% and nominated staff were trained as fire wardens and in the use of fire extinguishers.

The service offered mixed-sex accommodation. Each client had access to their own bedroom with an en-suite bathroom. Clients had keys to their rooms and could lock them when not in use. All clients could lock their rooms from the inside. There were 2 double occupancy rooms, and the service had now implemented a risk assessment for room sharing. Staff audited whether this risk assessment had been carried out and took actions where an audit showed improvements in this area were needed. We saw that 1 client had declined to share a room and opted to have a single room, based on their needs and preferences.

The service environment was functional and appropriately furnished. Staff carried out regular environmental risk assessments and completed relevant training. Staff received training in health, safety and welfare and compliance was 88%.

There were appropriate arrangements to monitor gas safety. Following our feedback, managers said they would place an additional carbon monoxide detector in the kitchen area.

The service regularly assessed potential ligature risks in the environment and had policies to mitigate these risks. This included individual risk assessments, risk management plans and different levels of observations for clients with different needs. Ligature cutters were easily accessible and staff knew where these were.

The service had access to emergency medicines which staff checked and stored appropriately. There was also a defibrillator available with instructions for use. First aid kits and body fluid spillage kits were available, with contents which were in date. The staff carried out monthly medical equipment audits, with over 94% compliance in the 6 months before our inspection.

Non-alcohol-based hand sanitiser was now provided in communal areas. We raised this in our previous inspections as this could pose risks to clients admitted for alcohol treatment.

Clients could raise maintenance issues in weekly community meetings. Clients told us that some issues had been fixed while some still required attention, for example water leaking from a shower onto a bedroom floor.

There was adequate space for the number of clients within the service, including a group and individual therapy rooms. There was a communal bathroom available on the ground floor which had a bath that clients could use. There was a garden that was accessible to clients with a covered table and seating area.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Safe systems, pathways and transitions

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service did not work well with people and health system partners to establish and maintain safe systems of care. They did not manage or monitor people’s safety effectively. They did not make sure there was continuity of care, including when people moved between different services.

The service received referrals from self-funding clients. The admission process was designed to ensure that essential information about the client was received. The service now had an admission policy with clear inclusion and exclusion criteria that it considered against each referral. Prior to admission, clients underwent a consultation to determine their suitability for the service.

During our assessment we found that 2 clients were admitted to the service despite meeting its exclusion criteria. This meant that the needs of these clients exceeded those that the service was able to meet safely. Additionally, the decision to continue one of these admissions was made by a staff member who had no clinical qualifications.

Staff did not involve all the necessary healthcare services to ensure patients had continuity of safe care, both within the service and post-discharge. Two clients were admitted to the service without a summary from their GP to verify their medical history prior to admission, and there was no record of the risks of this being clearly discussed with the clients. This was not in line with best practice guidance and the provider’s own admission policy which stated that staff must do all they can to obtain a GP summary on the day of admission. Because not all healthcare providers were aware of the clients’ changing physical health needs and potential drug interactions, this increased the risk of avoidable harm.

We saw evidence that discharge planning had improved. For example, 1 client was discharged with appropriate relapse prevention medications prescribed. Staff told us about giving clients harm minimisation advice and discussing any safeguarding issues on discharge. Naloxone (a life-saving medication used to rapidly reverse an opioid overdose) was provided to those at risk of experiencing an overdose. In 3 of 4 care records, there was evidence of planning for an unexpected treatment exit. There was an aftercare offer available which consisted of 3 follow-up calls with a therapist and weekly online meetings. Leaders told us they were planning to improve this provision further by developing a carer offer.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Safeguarding

evidenceCategory.commentary:
Although most staff were up to date with appropriate training and governance around safeguarding practice had been improved since our last inspection, safeguarding incidents were not always managed robustly or clearly identified by the staff group.

The provider’s systems to act on allegations or evidence of abuse needed further strengthening. Although staff recently reported a sexual safety incident involving a client and a member of staff, no further action was taken. The incident was not considered for a further safeguarding discussion. There was also no clear management plan for client and staff safety, and no evidence of consideration for referral or statutory notification to external bodies. Registered providers must notify CQC about certain incidents that affect people using or working within their service.

Staff had received mandatory safeguarding training. All staff were up to date with safeguarding adults and children levels 1 and 2. Compliance with level 3 training was 88% and compliance with preventing radicalisation was 95%. The service had appointed a safeguarding lead, however they had not yet completed the designated safeguarding lead training.

Since our last inspection, governance around reviewing safeguarding processes had been put in place. Staff completed a monthly safeguarding audit which examined the details and management of safeguarding concerns.

Information about safeguarding, boundaries and sexual safety was included in the client welcome pack.

Staff we spoke with demonstrated awareness of how to recognise individuals at risk of or suffering harm. Staff knew how to report their concerns. The safeguarding lead shared examples of discussing relevant cases with the local authority. However, although we saw that safeguarding was discussed in a recent team meeting, most staff could not share examples of recent safeguarding cases and how these were managed.

Staff followed safe arrangements for people visiting clients at the service. Rooms were available that could be reserved for visits, or visits could take place off-site.

There were some restrictions in place within the service, which were proportionate and necessary to maintain a healthy and safe environment. These were now clearly outlined in the client welcome pack. For example, no psychoactive substances or gambling were permitted on the premises.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

keyQuestionRatings.name: Well-led
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
This means we looked for evidence that service leadership, management and governance assured high-quality, person-centred care; supported learning and innovation; and promoted an open, fair culture.

At our last assessment we rated this key question inadequate. At this assessment the rating has changed to requires improvement.

The service was in breach of regulation in relation to good governance. The provider had made significant improvements in governance procedures and a change in operational leadership at the service. However, areas for further improvement remained. There was no clinical lead role within the service to oversee and drive continuous improvement and provide expert knowledge and guidance on best practice to the team.
keyQuestionRatings.narrative: This service is not always well-led

topicareas.name: Capable, compassionate and inclusive leaders

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service had inclusive leaders who understood the context in which they delivered care, treatment and support and embodied the culture and values of their workforce and organisation. Leaders had the skills, knowledge, experience and credibility to lead effectively. They did so with integrity, openness and honesty.

Since our last inspection, the service had appointed new operational leaders. The new Registered Manager and Nominated Individual had the skills, knowledge and competence to perform their roles. There was also a new deputy manager. During this inspection, we saw improvements in the service’s governance systems. The new managers demonstrated a good understanding of the service they managed and of the areas that still needed improving.

Staff we spoke with described the leaders as supportive and approachable, although some staff thought the leaders could be more visible at the service and that communication could be improved.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Freedom to speak up

evidenceCategory.commentary:
There were ways that staff could speak up about areas that concerned them, but it was not always clear how this information was acted upon and staff said they did not always see changes happen as a result.

Staff we spoke with said they were comfortable to raise concerns with managers if needed. However, 2 staff members did not think that changes happened in response to the issues they had raised.

Clients had opportunities to give feedback on the care they received. The service organised weekly community meetings and collected feedback from clients. We saw examples of changes made as a result of complaints.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Governance, management and sustainability

evidenceCategory.commentary:
Although there had been significant improvements with the governance processes since our last inspection, there were areas where these needed to be fully embedded to ensure the service was delivered to a consistently high standard.

At this inspection, we saw tangible improvements since our last inspection in the service’s governance systems and in how staff used them. The new operational managers demonstrated a good understanding and oversight of the service. Staff we spoke with said that the improvements in governance and processes had led to clearer documentation and more streamlined working. They said they were now clear on what they needed to do in their role. Staff said that checklists and documentation were now clearer and helpful to support them in their roles.

There was now a framework of what must be discussed in staff and managers’ meetings, such as incidents and complaints. Although gaps in managing incidents remained, there was now assurance that there was a functional system in place to report them and staff discussed essential information. We saw evidence of changes made as a result of learning. The service recognised that there was more work to do to strengthen all staff understanding of when something should be reported as an incident.

The service had improved its systems to manage risk. There were now a risk register and a business continuity plan in place. The risk register detailed an appropriate range of risks specific to the service and mitigations for these. Environmental risk management had improved, including improvements in fire safety and security of the premises.

There were now appropriate policies and procedures in place, including clear inclusion and exclusion criteria for admissions to the service. The discharge planning process had improved. The service had implemented a range of audits to provide assurance of the quality and safety of the service. The service now provided its staff with induction, competency assessments, training, managerial supervision and appraisal. The service collected data such as outcome measures. Managers had access to information needed to support them with their role, such as audits, performance, and staffing data.

However, despite the improvements made in governance processes, there was more work to be done to ensure the service always delivered safe and effective care. Some areas of risks remained, and some areas of governance still needed improving.

Care and treatment was not always provided safely and in line with the provider’s policies and national best practice guidance. Although staff now completed audits, in the absence of clinical governance structures, it was not clear whose role it was to follow up any actions identified. This meant there was limited assurance that audit results could be used to monitor and continuously improve the safety and quality of medically assisted treatments offered. There was a lack of clarity about the roles and responsibilities of the sessional doctors the service employed. Doctors did not attend team meetings, which limited effective information sharing about patient risk and clinical decision-making.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Learning, improvement and innovation

evidenceCategory.commentary:
Whilst there were early plans to develop aspects of the service, these were not yet implemented in practice.

Managers told us about plans to improve and develop some aspects of the service, including the therapy programme, aftercare, and provision for carers.

A range of audits was now in place, and we saw evidence where this had led to improvements in practice.

The service did not participate in research, quality improvement, benchmarking, or accreditation schemes at the time of our inspection.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Partnerships and communities

evidenceCategory.commentary:
Whilst the service did link with some external services, this was an area for further development.

The service did not routinely work with external partner agencies. Managers told us about plans to develop some joint working in the future.

However, we saw evidence that staff had referred clients to more appropriate care when required, for example to the emergency department at a local acute hospital. A recently discharged client we spoke with told us about their discharge plan which included information on available community support. Clients could provide feedback to the provider’s leadership team through weekly community meetings.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Shared direction and culture

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service did not have a clear shared vision, strategy and culture.

Recent changes in leadership meant there had been limited time for leaders to develop and embed a clear culture, vision and strategy at the service. Meeting minutes we reviewed did not document discussions about vision, values, or strategy, and it was not clear how the provider monitored its progress against those. Staff had limited opportunities to contribute to discussions about the strategy and development for the service. A lack of clinical leadership, and therefore expert clinical guidance in the team, meant there was no one with the appropriate clinical background and knowledge driving and ensuring high standards of patient care, supporting staff development, and safe, effective, and evidence-based practice.

Although there were now monthly team meetings, they had not taken place every month, and not all staff attended those. Some staff we spoke with said that communication and information sharing within the service could be improved.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Workforce equality, diversity and inclusion

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service valued diversity in their workforce. They worked towards an inclusive and fair culture by improving equality and equity for people who work for them.

The service had now ensured that staff received mandatory training in equality, diversity, and human rights, and 94% of staff had completed it.

Staff said they thought the service was open and inclusive and did not raise any concerns about discrimination.

Staff we spoke with did not require any reasonable adjustments to enable them to carry out their roles. Some said they found the service approach generally flexible, for example in shift allocation or hybrid working.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care
